off.p: For trains travelling entirely within Switzerland, passport/visa checks are not a routine part of the journey, though police checks can occur. I couldn’t find a reliable published frequency, so I wouldn’t put a percentage on the chance of being checked.

off.p: Yes—grounding an entire aircraft type can cause noticeable cancellations. Airlines have ways to reduce the disruption, but they generally cannot replace every grounded aircraft immediately. The cancellation figures in your update are consistent with that.

Airlines plan for individual aircraft becoming unavailable through maintenance or breakdowns, using spare aircraft and flexibility in their schedules. Losing a whole type at once can exceed that allowance—and any spare aircraft of the grounded type are unusable too.
Their main options are to:

off.li: Reassign other aircraft and use available spare capacity.
Keep older aircraft that were due to retire or leave the fleet.
Lease replacements, sometimes with crews supplied by another operator—a *wet lease*.
Combine departures using larger aircraft, reduce frequencies, and rebook passengers.
Cancel flights or postpone new routes when those measures are insufficient.

off.p: For a concrete example, Air Canada reported protecting 96% of its planned flying after the 2019 MAX grounding. It extended leases on six existing aircraft, accelerated the arrival of replacement aircraft, contracted other carriers, and combined some frequencies onto larger aircraft. It still suspended some routes and delayed some launches. Air Canada’s first-quarter 2019 report

Replacement capacity also has limits: the aircraft needs suitable range and capacity, qualified crews, and maintenance support. When many airlines simultaneously seek replacements, they are competing for the same available aircraft.

The important factor is the airline’s dependence on the grounded type, rather than the country’s size. A small airline with only a few MAX aircraft might lose a large fraction of its capacity. A much larger airline could absorb the same number more readily. Southwest, for example, said its 34 MAX aircraft accounted for less than 5% of daily flights when the grounding began. It subsequently reported approximately 2,800 MAX-related cancellations through the end of March 2019. Southwest’s grounding statement, March 27 operating update

For travellers, the effect is therefore uneven: many flights operate normally, while particular routes lose departures or require different connections. A flight originally scheduled on another aircraft can also be affected if that aircraft is reassigned to cover a grounded plane’s route.

Duration matters, too. A short grounding mainly requires immediate substitutions and rebooking. A prolonged grounding forces airlines to rewrite schedules, and missed deliveries can further reduce planned capacity. Southwest ultimately deferred aircraft retirements to cover part of that deficit. Southwest’s 2019 results

on.p: Yes. Grounding a whole aircraft type causes noticeable disruption, with the severity depending on how much of each airline’s operating capacity it removes. Aircraft on order matter mainly for future schedules; aircraft already flying determine the immediate impact.
Airlines have ways to recover from aircraft shortages, but their spare capacity is finite. They can:

on.li: Reassign available aircraft and adjust flight times.
Consolidate departures, carrying passengers on fewer flights.
Extend leases or postpone planned aircraft retirements.
Hire aircraft with crews from another operator—a *wet lease*.
Cancel flights and rebook passengers.

on.p: Air Canada provides a concrete example. On March 19, 2019, it announced that it could cover 98% of its planned flying through April 30, using aircraft substitutions, lease extensions and accelerated introduction of acquired aircraft. Some routes were temporarily suspended. This illustrates how much airlines can recover through changes to their fleets and schedules. Air Canada’s announcement

Those measures have limits. Replacement aircraft need suitable capacity and range, qualified crews and availability. When many airlines seek replacements simultaneously, hiring aircraft becomes harder. An aircraft also typically operates several flights each day, so losing one can affect multiple departures.

The cancellations in your update show the remaining shortfall. Southwest’s March 27 filing estimated approximately 2,800 MAX-related cancellations through March 31, after grounding 34 aircraft. Southwest’s filing

Country size is a weak predictor. The important factors are the affected airline’s dependence on the type and the alternative services available to passengers. Losing a few departures on a frequently served route may mean a later flight; losing the only daily service can mean a substantial delay.

Finally, the disruption can reach flights originally scheduled on other aircraft. Airlines move those aircraft to cover selected MAX routes, then cancel flights elsewhere. American explicitly described this in its passenger guidance. Checking the aircraft type on your booking therefore cannot establish whether your flight will be affected. American’s explanation

off.p: Yes, it could be a problem—but denial is not automatic. Visiting a boyfriend or girlfriend is generally a permitted B‑2 purpose, provided the visit is temporary. CBP still decides whether to admit her; a visa does not guarantee entry. State Department guidance

off.p: A finding of material misrepresentation can cause permanent inadmissibility, although waivers are available in some circumstances. Being truthful at the border does not automatically erase an earlier material lie. State Department explanation

She should answer CBP truthfully. If she deliberately denied an existing relationship, she should consult a U.S. immigration attorney before traveling, giving them the exact interview question, her answer, and the relationship timeline.

The key issue is whether her answer was true when she gave it:

In your situation, concealing the relationship could potentially have prevented questions about her intention to return home. That requires an assessment of the actual facts. off.p: Yes—some services advertise exactly this, although automatic buying is less common than price alerts. What you describe is essentially a flight *limit order*.

table: Says you select a flight, set your target price and authorize payment. It checks every 15 minutes and automatically books and charges your card when the target is reached.
Advertises target prices, itinerary constraints and optional automatic booking attempts. It is a beta/early-access service, listed at $99/year, and requires your own supported flight-data API key.
Lets you specify a target price, airports, date window, trip length, stops and airlines. It alerts you; you make the purchase.

off.p: Those automatic-booking descriptions are the providers’ own claims; I haven’t tested a purchase or independently established their reliability.
As for why this isn’t standard everywhere, the evidence points to practical and industry hurdles rather than a special prohibition on target-price purchases:

off.li: A search price needs confirmation. Amadeus’s booking workflow explicitly checks the latest price and availability before booking. A service finding a fare below your threshold still has to secure it before it disappears. Amadeus documentation

“Meets my criteria” can be complicated. Baggage, refundability, connections, airports and departure times all matter. My inference is that automatic buying needs much tighter instructions than an alert does; otherwise it can buy a cheap ticket you wouldn’t actually choose. DOT’s explanation of ticket differences

Issuing tickets adds operational obligations. For example, Amadeus requires production booking customers to meet local legal requirements and work with a ticketing consolidator. Changes and refunds then require support through that consolidator. Amadeus booking FAQ
Some major search sites don’t sell the ticket. KAYAK identifies itself as a search engine rather than a booking provider, so adding automatic purchase would extend its role considerably. KAYAK help

off.p: Your idea is feasible. The critical feature to look for is a hard maximum on the final total, including required fees and baggage, alongside precise itinerary constraints—and clear handling when the fare changes before booking.

on.p: Yes—some services advertise automatic booking at a target price, though availability and booking rules vary. What you describe is essentially a *limit buy order* for a flight.
The closest examples I found are:

table: Advertises the exact workflow: choose a flight, set your target price, authorize your card, and let it automatically book when the fare reaches your target. I could verify its indexed description, but couldn’t confirm its current operation or supported airlines.

Describes rules covering route, dates, cabin, stops, passengers and a hard price ceiling, with optional automatic booking. It is accepting early-access requests, so treat this as an announced product.

Offers automatic booking after monitoring fares. Its domestic-flight terms require advance funding at the current fare and say it will eventually book even if the desired drop never happens. That differs from your “buy only below XXX” condition.

on.p: If an alert is sufficient, milo supports a target price plus criteria such as date windows, trip length, stops and airlines. You complete the purchase yourself.

The evidence points to booking and payment constraints, rather than a specific prohibition on the idea. I didn’t find a rule specifically banning conditional flight purchases. There are several concrete complications:

on.li: A displayed fare can change before purchase. Duffel’s airline-booking documentation explicitly says that retrieving an offer does not guarantee availability at booking, and that its price can change. An automatic buyer must recheck the final price and stop if it exceeds your limit. Duffel documentation

The service needs a way to issue tickets. For example, Amadeus requires users of its self-service booking API to contract with a ticketing consolidator before obtaining production access. Its requirements also include meeting local legal obligations. Amadeus FAQ

Charging your card later requires authorization and payment handling. Payment systems support merchant-initiated transactions under an agreement with the customer, but authentication requirements can complicate unattended purchases. Stripe’s explanation

Your criteria need to define the whole purchase. “Below $400” needs to specify whether that includes bags and fees, and which fare restrictions you accept. Booking APIs expose separate ancillary services and change/refund conditions, so the automation must evaluate those too. Duffel offer documentation

on.p: My inference is that these obligations help explain why alerts are easier to offer: automatic buying commits the service to executing and supporting a ticket purchase. The concept is feasible; the exact “buy below my ceiling, otherwise do nothing” behavior needs careful checking in each service’s terms.

off.p: Assuming you’re applying using your Italian passports:

off.li: Other-country passports or identity cards: Answer Yes and enter your Israeli passport details, using the passport number, not your Israeli national ID number. The question specifies identity cards “for travel”; an ordinary Israeli identity card is not an international travel document, so my reading is that you do not need to add it in this section. This distinction is also explained in this answer about the same question.

off.p: A separate field labelled “National Identification Number” is a different question—do not confuse it with the document-number field for another passport or travel identity card.

off.li: Your father’s employment: Answer Yes and report his current self-employment. He can enter SELF-EMPLOYED as the employer name and provide his business address, using his home address if that is where he works. He does not need to substitute his employer from 15 years ago. The CBP ESTA online help explicitly allows “self-employed” as an employment description.

on.p: Assuming you are applying with your Italian passports:

My reading is that your ordinary Israeli *Teudat Zehut* does not belong in that section. If you report a qualifying travel identity card, use its document number. Your father’s employment: Answer Yes and give his current self-employment details. Enter SELF-EMPLOYED in the employer-name field and provide his business address and contact information. He does not need to use the employer from 15 years ago. CBP’s ESTA help explicitly allows self-employment as employment information. ESTA Online Help, hosted by the U.S. government.

on.p: One current update: Israel now also participates in the Visa Waiver Program, subject to the passport and other eligibility requirements. Whichever passport you use for the ESTA application, use that same passport for travel to the United States. Official ESTA guidance.
